newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia rebels kill 10 soldiers in oil region.
newsitem.headline: Colombia rebels kill 10 soldiers in oil region.

text.p: Leftist rebels killed at least 10 troops and wounded 11 in fighting in an oil-rich region of northeast Colombia early on Friday, an army spokeswoman said.
The deaths come five days after guerrillas shot down a helicopter, killing 20 soldiers and one civilian, in the same area around the town of Arauquita in Arauca province.

In both incidents troops came under fire as they moved in to secure the zone after rebels twice dynamited the main oil pipeline which serves U.S. multinational Occidental Petroleum Corp's field in nearby Cano Limon.
"There are 10 soldiers dead and 11 others injured. The troops were carrying out operations in the area when the guerrillas attacked them," the spokeswoman said.

The dead were all members of an elite anti-guerrilla battalion, part of the army's Second Division. The killings, just outside the village of Agua Chica, were blamed on the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), Latin America's oldest and largest guerrilla army.

Unsourced intelligence reports, quoted by local media in recent days, suggest, however, that the FARC is working in conjunction with the smaller Cuban-inspired National Liberation Army (ELN) in the province.
The ELN, set up by radical Roman Catholic priests in 1966, specialises in attacks on Colombia's key oil infrastructure.

Carlos Rincon, mayor of Arauquita, close to the scene of Friday's clash, said an army plane had bombed and strafed the zone to flush out the guerrillas. But no rebel casualties have so far been reported, the army spokeswoman said.

The first attack on the pipeline that cuts through the region, pumping crude from Cano Limon to the Caribbean coast port of Covenas, took place on Sunday. Shortly afterward, ELN rebels shot down the chopper as it transported troops to the site of the detonation.

The second blast of the week, and the 37th this year, occurred early on Thursday forcing Occidental to shut down the Cano Limon field, which is one of the largest in the country and normally produces 180,000 barrels a day.
The recent spate of guerrilla attacks has thrown President Ernesto Samper's calls for a new peace process into doubt, political analysts say.

Army top brass insist Colombia's guerrillas, who have been fighting a low-scale insurgency for more than 30 years, must be defeated militarily while at the same time complaining they have neither sufficient manpower nor adequate equipment.
In a separate incident in northwest Antioquia province, soldiers killed three FARC insurgents as they attempted to hijack trucks close to the industrial city of Medellin.
